attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Will never know' is an unhedged forecast of permanent nondisclosure. The acquisition qualifier is kept. 'Revenues or costs' ordinarily means neither will be known.

contract.note: The plain reading (public knowledge of realized revenue or costs for a defined period) is fair. The accounting-basis clause is meant for monetary-amount claims. It does not apply here because the claim is about nondisclosure, and GAAP revenue in a filing is plainly 'true revenue'.

evidence.note: Company blog dated Aug 14, 2026 confirms the acquisition closed, so the antecedent is met. This is evidence of the condition, not the outcome.
SpaceX filing, available Oct 22, 2026 (before the evaluation date), discloses $608M of realized revenue attributable to Cursor for Aug 14 to Sep 30, 2026. Net income is not separately determinable.

reviews.rationale: The acquisition closed. Nine days after the post, SpaceX's filing publicly disclosed Cursor-specific realized revenue for a defined post-closing period, which meets the early-resolution rule. Costs were not separated out, but the claim denied that either revenue or costs would be known. A nondisclosure claim needs no matching accounting basis.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm general causal claim about AI businesses: more demand brings bigger losses, and the most engaged customers are the least profitable.

contract.note: Reading it as a general pattern rather than a literal universal is fair and ordinary. Asking for customer-level and representative evidence fits a claim this broad. The 2026 period is drawn from the context.

evidence.note: Secondary account saying Harvey's costs rose with usage, then recovered. It covers one company and gives no customer-level ranking.
Secondary fact-check of Harvey's reported return to positive gross margin after a model change. This is one company's exception and does not settle the general pattern.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only one company's anecdote: Harvey's margins fell after usage rose, then recovered after a model change. There is no representative causal evidence across AI businesses and no customer-level profitability ranking, so the general claim is neither established nor refuted.

attribution.note: The 5GW figure belongs to the reported investor statements. Only the 'no compelling evidence' assertion is Zitron's own.

semantics.note: First-person epistemic observation. The revision correctly keeps 'I can find no' and credits the 5GW figure to the NYT and investors.

contract.note: Testing operational capacity at end-2025 is a defensible reading of 'there was', but the speaker did not supply it. If future contracted capacity counted as 'for it to buy', the result could change. 'Compelling' has no set standard.

evidence.note: Epoch's pre-post estimate of about 1.4GW at end-2025 rests on a rival's possibly biased memo, which Epoch flags as uncertain. It is not verified operational capacity.
Oct 2025 company announcement: more than 1GW of TPU capacity expected online in 2026. This is prospective procurement, not capacity operating at end-2025.

reviews.rationale: The packet has an uncertain third-party estimate above 1GW and a prospective procurement deal. Neither credibly establishes at least 1GW of operational Anthropic capacity at end-2025, and nothing sets an upper bound below 1GW. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own description of what is publicly known.

semantics.note: Keeps the four-company scope, the FY2026 single year, the Bloomberg source and the stated derivation from the OpenAI disclosure.

contract.note: Excluding run rates and cloud totals fits the speaker's own context. 'Calculated from' is ordinarily read as the estimate's derivation, and the contract tests it that way.

evidence.note: TNW reports that Bloomberg's ~$34B FY2026 estimate came from extrapolating Microsoft's 123% growth rate. The OpenAI figure was only compared against it, not used to derive it.

Bloomberg's own report confirms a FY2026 estimate of realized AI revenue and says Microsoft disclosed only two run-rate figures. It also shows the estimate was built on growth, not on the OpenAI disclosure.
Amazon disclosed an AI run rate, not realized AI revenue, so under the contract it does not refute the claim.

reviews.rationale: This part holds: a Bloomberg FY2026 estimate of Microsoft's realized AI revenue exists, and Microsoft disclosed only run rates. Amazon gave only a run rate. This part fails: the estimate was extrapolated from a growth rate, not calculated from the OpenAI revenue disclosure. Google, Oracle and the 'single year' exclusivity were not fully checked.
